section_1.title: Introduction: The Intuition of Summing Randomness
section_1.content: Start with a 30-second hook: Imagine a robot assembly line where two independent robotic arms place parts. Arm A has a placement error (X1) and Arm B has an error (X2). If both follow a bell-shaped distribution, what does the total error (X1+X2) look like? Visualize two narrow bell curves sliding together.
section_1.example: A delivery drone experiences random wind gusts (Distribution A) and sensor jitter (Distribution B). The total deviation from the target is the sum of these two independent random variables.

section_2.title: Prerequisites: Independence and Parameters
section_2.content: Quickly review that a Gaussian distribution N(μ, σ²) is defined by mean (μ) and variance (σ²). Define 'Independence': the outcome of one does not affect the other. This is the crucial constraint for the additive property.
section_2.example: If Arm A has μ=0, σ²=1 and Arm B has μ=0, σ²=2, these are two independent bells on a graph.

section_3.title: The Core Theorem: Adding the 'DNA'
section_3.content: Explain the visual transformation: When you add two independent Gaussian variables, the means add up (μ_total = μ1 + μ2) and the variances add up (σ²_total = σ²1 + σ²2). Show an animation where the two peaks merge into one wider, shifted peak.
section_3.example: The final distribution is N(μ1+μ2, σ²1+σ²2). Visually show the bell curve 'stretching' and 'sliding' on the X-axis.

section_4.title: Interactive Visualization: The Convolution Effect
section_4.content: Explain mathematically that the sum of two random variables is the 'convolution' of their probability density functions. Simplify this by showing the 'stacking' of probabilities. The result is always another bell curve—a unique feature of the Gaussian family.
section_4.example: Use a graphic of two overlapping transparent bell curves merging into a single, broader solid bell curve to illustrate the resulting distribution.

section_5.title: Application and Conclusion
section_5.content: Summarize that this property simplifies complex systems. We don't need complex calculus to find the final error; we just add the parameters. This is why Gaussian noise is so prevalent in nature and engineering.
section_5.example: In a smartphone camera, the final 'noise' in a photo is the sum of sensor thermal noise and signal processing interference—both Gaussians, resulting in one predictable Gaussian blur.
